subtopic_detail: Assessment and initial management of a paediatric iron overdose from prenatal multivitamins
stem:
You are the emergency department paediatric registrar. A 22 month old boy weighing 12 kg is brought in by his mother 90 minutes after she found him with an open bottle of her prenatal iron tablets (ferrous sulfate 325 mg, providing 65 mg elemental iron per tablet). The bottle originally contained 60 tablets and she estimates about 20 are missing. He has vomited twice on the way to hospital and there is a small amount of dark material in the emesis bag.

On arrival he is alert but pale and clingy. Pulse 148 per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degC. Capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally. Abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness. There is no haematemesis at present.

data_table.History: Ferrous sulfate 65 mg elemental per tablet, up to 20 tablets missing, ingestion 90 min ago in a 12 kg toddler
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, BP 92/54 mmHg, RR 30 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, pale, capillary refill 3 seconds centrally, mild epigastric tenderness, no haematemesis
data_table.Estimated dose: Up to 20 x 65 mg = 1300 mg elemental iron, approximately 108 mg/kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Obtain an abdominal radiograph and a serum iron level drawn at 4 to 6 hours after ingestion to guide the need for intravenous deferoxamine chelation and whole bowel irrigation
options.rationale: Ingested elemental iron above 60 mg/kg is potentially toxic; abdominal radiograph may show radiopaque tablets and a 4 to 6 hour post ingestion serum iron guides chelation. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Perform gastric lavage now with a wide bore orogastric tube and give activated charcoal 1 g per kg via the tube once the airway has been secured
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not adsorb iron and gastric lavage is not routinely recommended; whole bowel irrigation is considered if radiopaque tablets are visible. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Give intravenous deferoxamine 15 mg per kg per hour empirically now before any serum iron result and continue until vomiting settles and vital signs normalise
options.rationale: Empirical deferoxamine is reserved for severe symptoms or shock; peak level at 4 to 6 hours guides use rather than routine empirical therapy. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Discharge home with oral rehydration advice and a general practitioner review in 24 hours after a normal capillary blood glucose and one hour of asymptomatic observation in the department
options.rationale: Symptomatic ingestion with tachycardia, pallor and vomiting requires observation and iron level; discharge at 1 hour misses the delayed toxic phase. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Administer oral N acetylcysteine 150 mg per kg over one hour and repeat the loading dose every 4 hours for two further cycles to reduce hepatic iron induced oxidative injury
options.rationale: N acetylcysteine is used for paracetamol not iron toxicity; there is no role in acute iron overdose beyond compassionate use. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Paediatric iron overdose progresses in five phases starting with gastrointestinal irritation within 6 hours, then a latent phase, followed by shock and metabolic acidosis, hepatotoxicity and finally gastric outlet obstruction. Ingested elemental iron above 20 mg/kg produces symptoms, above 60 mg/kg is potentially toxic, and above 150 mg/kg is potentially lethal. Assessment includes abdominal radiograph looking for radiopaque tablets and a serum iron level at 4 to 6 hours post ingestion. Deferoxamine 15 mg per kg per hour is indicated for serum iron above 90 micromol/L, shock, acidosis or altered conscious state. Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol is considered if the radiograph shows visible tablets.
key_points: Assessment: abdominal radiograph and serum iron level 4 to 6 hours after ingestion.
Deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/h for shock, coma, acidosis or iron level above 90 micromol/L.
Activated charcoal does not adsorb iron; consider whole bowel irrigation if tablets are visible on abdominal radiograph.
explanation.pearls: Paediatric iron ingestion above 60 mg/kg elemental requires abdominal radiograph and serum iron at 4 to 6 hours; deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hour intravenous if level above 90 micromol/L or shock.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and first line management of paediatric anaphylaxis to peanut in a school aged child
stem:
You are the on call emergency registrar. A 7 year old girl weighing 24 kg is brought in by ambulance 20 minutes after taking one bite of a peanut butter sandwich at a friend's house. Within 5 minutes she developed generalised urticaria, lip swelling and repeated non productive cough. Ambulance officers documented facial angioedema and audible wheeze.

On arrival she is anxious and speaking in short phrases. Pulse 138 per minute, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 per minute, oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degC. There is widespread urticaria over the trunk and limbs, marked periorbital swelling, and audible bilateral wheeze with tracheal tug. There is no stridor. She has a documented previous mild reaction to peanut but has not been prescribed an adrenaline autoinjector.

data_table.History: Peanut ingestion 20 min ago, previous mild peanut reaction, no autoinjector prescribed
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 34 /min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Widespread urticaria, periorbital angioedema, bilateral wheeze, tracheal tug, short phrases, weight 24 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg per kg bolus and nebulised salbutamol 5 mg via oxygen mask, and defer adrenaline unless respiratory arrest or stridor develops during the next 10 minutes
options.rationale: Corticosteroids and bronchodilators do not treat anaphylaxis; delaying intramuscular adrenaline increases mortality. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 300 microgram (0.3 mL of 1:1000) into the mid anterolateral thigh and repeat every 5 minutes if symptoms persist while preparing intravenous access
options.rationale: Adrenaline intramuscular by ASCIA banded weight table is first line; 20 to 50 kg receives 300 microgram (EpiPen), repeat every 5 min if needed. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Give intravenous adrenaline 10 microgram per kg (240 microgram) as a slow bolus over 5 minutes through a peripheral cannula while a colleague establishes continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia
options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis in a monitored setting; first line is intramuscular for a child not in arrest. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Give oral cetirizine 10 mg with intravenous fluid support and observe for a further 4 hours in the short stay unit for a biphasic reaction before making a discharge decision
options.rationale: Oral antihistamine treats urticaria but not airway compromise or hypotension; anaphylaxis mandates intramuscular adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 150 microgram (0.15 mL of 1:1000) into the deltoid muscle and repeat only if there is no improvement in blood pressure within 10 minutes of the initial dose
options.rationale: 150 microgram dose is for 10 to 20 kg; a 24 kg child receives 300 microgram, and thigh (vastus lateralis) is preferred over deltoid. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction defined by acute onset of skin or mucosal involvement plus either respiratory compromise or hypotension. Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh is the single first line intervention and delaying it increases mortality. The ASCIA banded weight table sets dose by weight class: 7.5 to 10 kg receives 150 microgram, 10 to 20 kg receives 150 microgram (EpiPen Jr), 20 to 50 kg receives 300 microgram (EpiPen), above 50 kg receives 300 to 500 microgram. Adjuncts include supine positioning, high flow oxygen, intravenous fluid bolus 20 mL/kg for hypotension and nebulised salbutamol for wheeze. Antihistamines and corticosteroids treat associated urticaria but neither prevents nor treats anaphylaxis.
key_points: IM adrenaline anterolateral thigh is first line; ASCIA banded weight table dosing.
20 to 50 kg receives 300 microgram (0.3 mL of 1:1000) IM; repeat every 5 minutes if needed.
Corticosteroids and antihistamines are adjuncts and never replace adrenaline in anaphylaxis.
explanation.pearls: For paediatric anaphylaxis 20 to 50 kg give intramuscular adrenaline 300 microgram (0.3 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes as needed.
